intro: Bach’s Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565, opens with a flourish, a rest and a chord built up from the bass. Norbert Schenk plays the complete work on the organ of the Evangelische Kirche in Solms-Albshausen.

sections.label: Intro · Flourishes and held chords
sections.mNote: Octave runs alternate with pauses over the pedal bass.

sections.label: A · Fugue subject in semiquavers
sections.mNote: The semiquaver subject passes between the organ’s voices.

sections.label: B · Fugue entries and episodes
sections.mNote: Entries of the running subject alternate with shorter episodes.

sections.label: C · Recitative passages and broad chords
sections.mNote: Free flourishes interrupt the fugue’s steady motion.

sections.label: Coda · D minor and the church
sections.mNote: The organ’s sound continues after the closing chord.

cues.title: Opening flourish and diminished-seventh chord
cues.text: The organ opens with a mordent on its first note, pauses, then descends in octaves. Over a held low D, a diminished-seventh chord is built up one note at a time.
cues.evidence: Opening of BWV 565: octave doubling, mordent and diminished-seventh chord over D. Netherlands Bach Society: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-565. Harmonic description: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fugue subject and exposition
cues.text: The fugue’s subject is made entirely of semiquavers. It returns repeatedly to a fixed note, an implied pedal, while a second melodic line falls and rises around it. Other voices then take up the subject in turn.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, fugue subject and exposition; the implied pedal note and melodic line are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Johannes Ringk’s copy
cues.text: The earliest surviving copy bears the name of Johannes Ringk. On the title page he wrote Toccata con Fuga and named Bach. Inside, the pedal part is written on the keyboard staves, and small letters mark where the feet play.
cues.evidence: Johannes Ringk manuscript, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 595; pedal notes marked p. The copy’s date is disputed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565

cues.title: Coda, Recitativo
cues.text: The closing section leaves behind the steady semiquavers of the fugue. It is marked Recitativo and moves in runs, pauses and broad chords. Several changes of tempo lead to the final Molto adagio and the close in D minor.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, seventeen-bar coda, marked Recitativo and ending Molto adagio with a minor plagal cadence. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
